title: Six days, then stop
hook: six days shalt thou labor, but the seventh is a sabbath (Exodus 20:9–10)

segments.voice: Yesterday, honest sweat: a field that fights back, and bread earned with the body. Your line was tired arms, real bread. What made you sweat? Day eight hundred eighty-two.

A list that never ends. Answer one message and two more arrive. Clear the sink and it's full again by evening. Work, left to itself, has no edge. So the Ten Commandments draw one: “Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God.” Work, and then a wall across the week, the same wall for everyone. Today: six days.
screen: `A LIST THAT NEVER ENDS.` → `WORK HAS NO EDGE.` → `SO THE COMMANDMENT DRAWS ONE.`

segments.voice: First, notice both halves. The commandment doesn't only say stop. It says labor, six days, and do all thy work. Work and rest arrive as one command, two sides of a single rhythm. Second, notice who gets to stop. The verse keeps going: “thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates.” The rest isn't a perk for the owner. The servant stops. The cattle stop. The outsider stops. Rest here is a kind of fairness, written into the week. Third, the reasons. In Exodus, the reason is creation: God made heaven and earth in six days and rested on the seventh. When the commandments are given again in Deuteronomy, the reason changes: “remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt.” People who once worked without end are told to build a week that ends. Fourth, how it's kept. Jews who keep Shabbat mark it from Friday evening to Saturday night, with candles, a meal, and a day set apart from work. Christians who keep Sunday call it the Lord's day, while Seventh-day Adventists keep Saturday. The shapes differ. The edge is the point. And since it's the end of a week, a look back: a thread on a wrist, many loves, love as a practice, then work. Where the hours go. A garden to tend and keep. Honest sweat. And now the stop that keeps all of it human.
screen: `WORK AND REST, ONE COMMAND.` · `THE STOP IS FOR EVERYONE.` · `CREATION, THEN EGYPT: TWO REASONS.` · `THE EDGE IS THE POINT.` · then, large: `SIX DAYS, THEN STOP.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Bring to mind the shape of your coming week: the shifts, the deadlines, the errands, the people waiting on you. Now look for an edge. Not a whole day, if a whole day isn't possible. An evening. A morning. A few hours. Choose one. Picture it clearly: what will you put down? The laptop, the phone, the list. Then ask the commandment's second question: who else could stop with you? Someone in your house. Someone who works for you. Hold that stopping time until it feels real enough to keep. If you pray, you can hold it in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Six days. From the Ten Commandments: six days of work, then a seventh set apart, for everyone within the gates. Today's word.
Your line: fairness, written into the week. Today, put your stopping time for this week on a calendar, and tell one person about it. Day eight hundred eighty-two.
